newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG's Chan says he initially opposed mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: PNG's Chan says he initially opposed mercenaries.

text.p: Former Papua New Guinea prime minister Sir Julius Chan, who stepped aside in March after an army revolt over plans to use mercenaries on Bougainville, on Wednesday said he initially opposed the use of foreign soldiers.

Begining his evidence to a judicial inqiury into his failed US$36 million mercenary plan, Chan said he rejected the first proposal presented to him in September 1996 by the British-based military consultancy Sandline International.
Chan said he changed his mind and agreed to hire the 70 African soldiers because of an increase in secessionst rebel activity on Bougainville island in late 1996.
Five PNG soldiers are still being held hostage by rebels after an attack in September 1996 which killed 11 soldiers at the Kangu Beach government base in southern Bougainville.
Chan said that he told mercenary leader Tim Spicer, chief executive of Sandline, of his opposition to foreign soldiers on the frontline when they met in Port Moresby on January 7, 1997.
"I said I would oppose any foreign armies being brought into PNG to kill Papua New Guinea citizens," said Chan.
"They (mercenaries) would work as advisers and backroom support people," he said.
Chan said that, even though the Sandline contract signed on January 31 stipluated mercenaries would be used in "offensive operations", the plan was still to only to use them as advisers.
He said it would be up to the discretion of the PNG army commander whether to use the African soldiers in fighting roles.
Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, sacked in March as army chief after calling on Chan to resign over the mercenary deal, has told the inquiry he always opposed the use of mercenaries.
The inquiry has been told that the plan to use mercenaries to end the nine-year-old Bougainville conflict was hatched in April 1996 in a coffee shop in the Australian town of Cairns.

At that meeting were Spicer, a former British lieutenant colonel and Scots Guard turned mercenary, Singirok, the then defence minister Mathias Ijape and international mining entrepreneur Tony Buckingham.
A series of subsequent clandestine meetings in London, Hong Kong and Port Moresby led to the 10-page mercenary contract being signed in Port Moresby on January 31.
On March 17, Singirok went on national radio and called on Chan to resign within 48 hours over the mercenary deal, which he labelled corrupt.
Chan immediately sacked Singirok, sparking an army revolt which resulted in two days of violence and looting and eventually Chan stepping aside pending the mercenary inquiry.
